## My approach

I lead AI transformation at two levels: setting the strategy with the CEO and executive team, and working hands-on in the forward-deployed engineer’s role, building the first systems with the teams who will run them.

### Move AI from units of work to systems of work

AI on a unit of work, one step in one function, changes little while the handoffs around it stay the same. I redesign the system of work, the whole chain across functions, and measure it from the first request to the result.
Prime Now · I took the stores’ spreadsheets, then automated a matched catalog, forecasts and a daily stock upload. Out of stock at partner stores fell from 25% to 5%.

### Decide what “accurate” means before building

I start from the claim a customer will read, and choose the reference the model learns from and is judged against. When the labels are noisier than the claim allows, I change where the labels come from.
Halo Body · Training labels moved from experts’ eyes to clinical X-ray scans. Published error: 2.16 points, half that of the best smart scale tested.

### Put one customer measure above the model metrics

A model can beat its benchmarks while customers think the product does not work. I run one measure of the customer’s outcome for the whole system, and hold every model metric to it.
Alexa Shopping · I listened to 1,000 requests a week and wrote how each was judged. Success rose from about 50% to 85%.
All thirteen principles · Hands-on builds

Page: About Njenga Kariuki
Address: https://njenga.ai/about/

# Njenga Kariuki

I lead AI transformation across Vodacom FinTech Group, including M-PESA: 100M+ customers in eight markets and $2B+ revenue. I report to the CEO and am building the AI Center of Excellence.
Before that, I spent twelve years at Amazon and AWS building AI products and businesses from zero to one, in software, hardware and mobile apps, across e-commerce, connected devices, supply chain, health and life sciences. I led cross-functional organizations of 100+ engineers, scientists and product managers, directed a $100M+ a year AI investment portfolio, and delivered machine learning, computer vision and large language model capabilities at global scale. Most recently I led product for Amazon Bio Discovery, an agentic AI application for antibody design.
I hold a master’s degree from Stanford Graduate School of Business, and my research on AI’s global economic impact was published by the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI in 2025.
My approach · Patents and papers · Hands-on builds · Education

## My approach

I still work in the order my operations training taught me: define the problem, measure it, find the cause, fix it, keep it fixed.

### Building an AI product

01 · Prove the problem before the technology · I state the customer problem without naming the technology, and test it apart from the capability before we invest.
I look for a durable customer problem, one people had before the technology and will still have after it. At Amazon’s Health Computer Vision and AI organization, every new capability had to answer such a problem. We ran customer research and capability experiments side by side, and paused further investment when either lacked proof.
- Amazon Health AI The products that shipped moved clinic measures onto the phone: body fat, waist-to-hip ratio, and mobility, stability and posture.
- Alexa Map View Phone room scanning already existed; I restated the problem as whether a customer could easily map a home.
02 · Own the reference, starting from the claim · I decide what each model is trained and checked against, starting from the claim customers will read.
The reference decides what accurate means to a customer, so the one product leader accountable chooses it. A claim measured against a clinical instrument needs that instrument’s readings to learn from. When the labels are noisier than the claim allows, I change where the labels come from.
- Halo Body Training labels moved from fitness experts’ ratings by eye to clinical X-ray (DXA) scans.
- Halo Movement The target was the score a movement expert would give, later checked against motion capture and clinical tests.
03 · Measure perceived utility and build around it · I measure how accurate and useful a result feels to the customer, apart from how the model scores.
A model’s accuracy on benchmarks and the accuracy a customer perceives are separate measures. So I ask customers directly whether a result feels accurate, means something to them and leads them to act. Then I change the model and the interface together, and measure again.
- Halo Tone Raw chart positions, first shown with two presidents’ voices, were replaced by daily bars and words such as “Hopeful.”
- Halo Movement The top of the 0 to 100 scale became a product decision: very athletic people rarely scored above 90.
- Amazon Bio Discovery Checkpoints measured the interface and how useful scientists found it, beyond the models’ scores.
04 · Keep customer and model metrics in harmony · I run one customer measure for the whole system above model metrics that scientists can improve step by step, and keep the two aligned.
The customer measure sets the target for each component, because a customer experiences the whole system. Three components that are each 90% accurate leave about one user in four with a problem. Fast rounds of customer feedback keep the two measures moving together.
- Alexa Shopping Success on each shopping request, judged against my written scoring guide, became the top measure above model metrics.
- Alexa Map View We worked on ease and map accuracy in the same rounds, and the scan went one room at a time.
05 · Measure perceived value at 2 and 4 weeks · Novelty lifts a first rating, so I measure perceived value again weeks after first use.
In my essay of June 2024, I recommended a 4-week test, because engagement starts to drop by week 2. My preferred measure is the Sean Ellis test: how disappointed people would be if they could no longer use the product. Between model versions, small groups of people new to the product react to each change, so their comments shape the next version.
- Amazon Halo We measured the value Halo members saw at first use and again at about 2 and 4 weeks.
- Halo Movement Improvement after 2 weeks of exercises became the outcome measure, matching the program’s reassessment point.
06 · Be first-hand on annotation and labeling · I work on annotation and labeling myself, because a rising score cannot show me what changed for the customer.
Labeling shows me how a model improved, which improvement it was and how it ties to what customers notice. The scoring guide that others will label by comes from real interactions I have judged myself.
- Alexa Shopping I listened to 1,000 requests a week and judged each request and reply as success or failure.
- Halo Tone I defined what listener panels rated, from happy to sad and low to high energy; ratings became training labels.
- Prime Now I sat in the stores, asked for whatever data they had, and designed the catalog matching around it.
07 · Turn coarse feedback into named dimensions · I turn coarse customer feedback into named dimensions, each with a measure the team can improve.
Each dimension then enters the evaluation with its own measure, so the team can track it from one model version to the next. Some dimensions sit outside the model: in products with complex input steps, the input step is part of the quality customers perceive.
- Halo Tone Customers wanted to see how their voice varied, so that variation, dynamism, became a measured dimension.
- Halo Movement Customers wanted variety in live workout feedback, so dynamism became a measured dimension of the workouts.
- Halo Body The scan itself became a measured part of quality, and from August 2021 it worked in smaller rooms.
08 · Measure on real-world data, beyond lab demos · I judge models on data from real use, measured against the real outcome.
What people perceive in the lab and in daily life differs sharply. A demo on curated lab data is the easy part. Most of the work is moving it into daily use, and I plan for that from the start. The warning sign is a model that beats industry benchmarks while users think the product does not work.
- Prime Now Store stock changed daily, so each store got forecasts and an automated daily upload of its inventory.
- Halo Tone I measured the whole audio path in daily wear, band to phone, against the accuracy customers perceived.
- Amazon Bio Discovery In antibody design, lab measurements of binding became the reference; models’ confidence scores showed little correlation with them.
09 · Codify the measure-and-improve loop for others · I write down how we measure and improve, as scoring guides, procedures and standards, so others can run it without me.
The core team first agrees on what counts as an error, and writes an example set for each one. Any ambiguity in the core team grows once a labeling team applies the rules. Written rules let labelers agree with each other, and let other teams run the same measures.
- Alexa Shopping My error definitions, each with example cases, became the procedures that a team of 10 data analysts applied.
- Amazon Health AI Body fat, mobility and waist-to-hip ratio were each tested against a named clinical reference in a published study.
- M-PESA Africa A written standard for AI in work that moves money: every check still runs.

### Leading the organization that builds it

10 · Lead at two levels: the strategy and the work · I set the strategy with the CEO and executive team, and go hands-on in the work itself, in the forward-deployed engineer’s role.
A working prototype on a team’s own work shows what the technology can do. So I build the first version with the people who will run it. The executive work decides which chains of work change; the hands-on work shows how they can.
- M-PESA Africa I set the direction reporting to the CEO, and build the first versions with the teams that redesign each chain of work.
- Prime Now I learned to code to automate the stores’ uploads myself, before the system ran for every store.
- Alexa Shopping I listened to 1,000 shopping requests a week while leading the evaluation team.
11 · Change how the team itself works · I change how my own organization works in short cycles, and keep only the changes that hold up.
In Amazon’s health AI teams, a product manager, a designer and a group of engineers spent each Friday on one charter: “build something that won’t work.” At AWS, I made the product organization itself AI-native, from how we defined products to how we built them.
- Amazon Health AI Ideas from the Friday builds still had to pass the same two proofs before investment scaled.
- Amazon Bio Discovery Alongside the product, the organization moved to AI-native ways of defining and building products.
12 · Change what teams and people are measured on · People work toward what they are measured and promoted on, so I change the measures first.
At Prime Now, each new country was measured on revenue, a goal that did not reward growing two-hour delivery. I proposed measuring each country on its percentage growth instead, and leadership adopted it.
- Prime Now Each country’s goal moved from revenue to percentage growth.
- M-PESA Africa Each changed workflow is measured end to end, against a comparison group working the old way.
13 · Measure the whole time the customer waits · I measure the whole time a customer waits, because AI that speeds up one step changes little while the handoffs around it stay the same.
If AI halves a two-day step in a 10-day process, the customer waits nine days instead of 10. The other eight days are handoffs, approvals and waiting. So I measure from the first request to the result, and change the steps around the AI along with the step it speeds up.
- M-PESA Africa Where the time goes in one workflow: halving the waiting saves more than halving the work.
- Amazon Bio Discovery Bench scientists had waited for computational biologists to run models; Bio Discovery put both in one application.

- 2026 · US 12,586,583 · Patent · [Power state control of a device performing detection of voice in audio data](https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/12586583) · A wearable that learns when its wearer’s voice tends to start, and times its low-power sleep to match.

2026–today · Vodacom FinTech Group

# M-PESA Africa

AI transformation of mobile money and financial services, for 100M+ customers in eight African markets.
M-PESA in Safaricom’s app in Kenya, 2026: the home screen. · 1 / 3
Role
Managing Executive: AI, reporting to the CEO
Scale
100M+ customers in eight markets; $2B+ revenue
Now
End-to-end redesign of work under way across the group’s markets
I lead AI transformation across Vodacom FinTech Group, including M-PESA, reporting to the CEO. I set the direction, from single AI tasks to whole chains of work redesigned across functions, and I am building the AI Center of Excellence that holds every change to one standard. I also work hands-on with the teams, building the first versions of each redesigned chain of work.

## What I decided

### Set the strategy: from units of work to systems of work

A unit of work is one task in one function, done faster with AI. A system of work is the whole chain of steps, across functions, that a customer or a colleague waits on. The chain is what we redesign.

### Held AI to one standard: every check still runs

When AI changes work that moves people’s money, every check still runs, screening and fraud included. Legal, risk and compliance join from the start and keep their sign-off. AI assists people before it automates a step.

### Judged each change by two results

Time end to end, against a comparison group working the old way, and value that finance signs off. Each workflow then ends in a decision: scale it, continue, narrow it or stop.

## How it worked

Before

### Mobile money at scale, with most of the time spent waiting

Safaricom and Vodacom set up M-PESA Africa in 2020 to develop M-PESA, their mobile money service, as one platform. I own the AI roadmap for customer experience, revenue growth, risk, fraud and operational efficiency. I measure each workflow from the first request to the result, because most of its time is spent waiting between steps.
01 Units

### AI on one task changes little

AI that speeds up one task in one function leaves the handoffs around it as they were, so the customer still waits. We started there, with pilots inside single functions, and that work continues: it builds the skills and the proof.
02 Systems

### The whole chain, redesigned across functions

We bring together the functions that share a chain of work, then redesign it with AI and automate it end to end. That move is under way across the group’s markets. Which workflows, and their results, stay internal while the work runs.
03 Standard

### High-risk steps stay with a person

Steps with high compliance risk stay with a person. Legal, risk and compliance teams set the conditions for each change and keep their sign-off. Each market owns its results.
04 People

### The people who will use it

The AI Center of Excellence sets shared standards for AI across eight markets and trains the people who use them: Kenya, Tanzania, the DRC, Mozambique, Lesotho, Ethiopia, Egypt and South Africa.
A drawing of the idea.

Page: Amazon Bio Discovery | Njenga Kariuki
Address: https://njenga.ai/bio-discovery/

2025–2026 · AWS Applied AI, Life Sciences

# Amazon Bio Discovery

Scientists design antibodies with AI agents in one application, and partner labs test the designs.
Choosing the target protein, then asking for recommended binding sites. · 1 / 2
Role
Head of Product, AWS Applied AI, Life Sciences, from the start to the launch
Scale
Directed a cross-functional organization of 100+ engineers, scientists and product managers
Launched
14 April 2026, at the AWS Life Sciences Symposium in New York
I led product for Amazon Bio Discovery, an agentic AI application for antibody design, from its start to its launch on 14 April 2026, with an organization of 100+ engineers, scientists and product managers. Memorial Sloan Kettering said its launch campaign went from target to lab order in weeks.

## What I decided

### Set the bar at the scientists’ own work

Drug discovery scientists work at the frontier of their field, so my bar was a product that fit the way they already worked. Access to models was only the first step. Fitting them into daily work meant working closely with those scientists.

### Checked the interface and its usefulness

From my earlier products I brought frequent checkpoints on two things beyond the models: the interface, and how useful scientists found it. Our team ran a design campaign with Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK), and the scientists’ feedback shaped the product.

### Launched once the product met the bar

We checked each version against that bar and launched when the product met it. It opened on 14 April 2026 with AI agents and more than 40 biological AI models.

## How it worked

Before

### Months from a target to a candidate

A paper AWS published at launch put conventional antibody discovery at 6 to 12 months, from a target protein to the antibody chosen for development. Scientists had little control over where on the target an antibody would bind. Bench scientists knew the biology and waited for computational biologists to run the models.
Conventional discovery took 6 to 12 months from a target to the antibody chosen for development; with Bio Discovery, the launch campaign reached a lab order in weeks.
01 Ask

### The agent proposes where to bind

A scientist uploads a target protein and presses “Recommend hotspots,” and an AI agent proposes where on the protein to bind. The agent runs bioinformatics tools, and a language model turns their results into ranked regions, each with written evidence. On known antibody-target pairs, one of its top five regions overlapped the true binding site about 80% of the time.
The agent’s ranked binding regions on a target, each with its evidence and rationale.
02 Design

### Three models, 288,000 designs

In the campaign with MSK, three design models, each working a different way, produced 96,000 nanobody designs apiece: 288,000 in all. A nanobody is a small antibody. The run used 2,000 GPUs in two AWS regions.
A workflow built from models in the catalog, ready to publish for others to run.
03 Judge

### What a design must pass to reach a lab

A second agent ranked the designs on five scores at once and kept the best trade-offs, until 100,000 remained.
An illustration with two of the five scores: the agent kept the best trade-offs first, then the next best, until 100,000 remained.
04 Test

### Only a lab test confirms a binder

Twist Bioscience, a launch lab partner, made the DNA for 100,000 designs, and a first lab screen sent 116 on to a binding test. Of the 116, 46 were confirmed to bind the target.
Each lab result returns to the experiment that produced it and is checked before any model retrains on it. At launch, MSK said the campaign went from target to a lab order in weeks.
Sending selected designs to a partner lab, with cost and time estimates.

## The launch campaign, design by design

## Launch

At launch: candidate designs filtered to the ones sent for lab testing.
“Patients come here with a clock. We need results sooner.”
Nai-Kong Cheung of Memorial Sloan Kettering, in Amazon’s launch announcement
Amazon Bio Discovery opened on 14 April 2026 at the AWS Life Sciences Symposium in New York. Scientists could design with its agents and more than 40 models, and send designs to partner labs with cost and turnaround shown before ordering. Amazon named Bayer, the Broad Institute, Fred Hutch Cancer Center and Voyager Therapeutics as early adopters.

## What came next

On 10 August 2026, Novo Nordisk made AWS its preferred cloud provider and strategic AI partner, and said it would use Bio Discovery to identify drug targets and design therapies faster. In October 2026, NVIDIA and the University of Washington’s Institute for Protein Design released an open protein design model, “available today through partners including Amazon Bio Discovery.”

Page: Stanford AI Institute | Njenga Kariuki
Address: https://njenga.ai/ai-index-2025/

2024–2025 · Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI)

# Stanford AI Institute

Published research on AI’s global economic impact: AI investment, jobs, enterprise adoption and robots, measured from five sources.
The AI Index Report 2025, published 7 April 2025.
Role
Author of the text and analysis
Research
AI investment, jobs, enterprise adoption and robots
Published
7 April 2025, by Stanford HAI, in its [AI Index](https://hai.stanford.edu/assets/files/hai_ai-index-report-2025_chapter4_final.pdf)
I wrote the text and analysis of published research from the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI) on AI’s global economic impact: AI investment, jobs, enterprise adoption and robots. HAI published it on 7 April 2025 as the economy chapter of its AI Index, Stanford’s annual report on the state of AI.

## What I decided

### Measured the economy in five layers

The chapter measured AI in the economy in five layers, each from its own data source, LinkedIn and McKinsey among them: investment, job postings, hiring, company use and robot installations.

### Wrote it in two-week memo cycles

Until April 2025 I brought a memo of 4 to 6 pages to the team’s weekly meeting every two weeks, sometimes every week.

### Opened with ten findings, each with a comparison

Ten findings open the chapter, each with a claim, a number and a comparison. In 2024, US private AI investment reached $109.1 billion, nearly 12 times China’s $9.3 billion.

## How it worked

Before

### One chapter for what AI was doing to the economy

The AI Index is Stanford’s annual report on the state of AI, written for policymakers, executives, journalists and the public by HAI. In 2024 I joined it as a graduate researcher, and my assignment was the economy.
01 Define

### Each number rests on a printed rule

A posting counted as an AI job only if it named a skill on Lightcast’s list of AI skills. Robot data run a year behind, so the chapter reported installations for 2023.
“This chapter examines AI-related economic trends using data from Lightcast, LinkedIn, Quid, McKinsey and the International Federation of Robotics (IFR).” The chapter’s overview, page 3.

### Five layers, one year at a time

Each layer has its own source and its own units, from investment in AI to robot installations.
The data as a table
Five data sources, one for each layer: values as printed, 2018 to 2024
Measure, source and unit · 2018 · 2019 · 2020 · 2021 · 2022 · 2023 · 2024
Investment, Quid private AI investment, world, billions of US dollars · 43.10 · 58.18 · 73.79 · 145.40 · 113.01 · 104.34 · 150.79

02 Write

### New research, in the chapter within eight weeks

Anthropic published its study of how people used its Claude assistant on 10 February 2025, and eight weeks later it was a four-page highlight in the chapter.
“Text and analysis by Njenga Kariuki”: the chapter’s opening page.
03 Find

### Three layers, three comparisons

Global corporate AI investment reached $252.3 billion in 2024, up 25.5% from 2023. The share of survey respondents whose organizations used AI rose to 78%, from 55% in 2023. China installed 276,300 industrial robots in 2023, six times Japan’s number.
Global corporate investment in AI, 2013 to 2024.
04 Publish

### The chapter and its data go out together

The chapter runs 77 pages, with 89 figures and an appendix on where each measure comes from. Each chart carries a source line, and the chart data are published as public files.
“U.S. private AI investment hit $109.1 billion in 2024, nearly 12 times higher than China’s $9.3 billion…” The third of the chapter’s highlights, page 4: a claim, a number and a comparison.

In October 2025, a Federal Reserve Board research note reproduced the chapter’s data on private AI investment and credited the 2025 AI Index. Alexa Map View
2023–2024

---

Page: Alexa Map View | Njenga Kariuki
Address: https://njenga.ai/map-view/

2023–2024 · Alexa Smart Home, Amazon

# Alexa Map View

A phone scan becomes a floor plan of the home, with every smart device on it, controlled from the map.
Amazon’s Map View film, 2023: scan a room, then control a device from the map.
Role
Led the Alexa app’s smart home features and took Map View to launch
Scale
50M+ monthly users of the app’s smart home features
Launched
November 2023, in the United States
I led the Alexa app’s smart home features, used by 50M+ people a month, and took Map View to launch in November 2023: a phone scan becomes a floor plan with every device on it. The mapping technology existed; the problem I owned was ease.

## What I decided

### Named ease as the hard problem

Phones could already measure a room: the iPhone 12 Pro gained LiDAR in 2020, and Apple gave developers a room-scanning tool in 2022. The question I owned was whether a customer could map a whole home.

### Set a measured bar for ease

Customers rated “Scanning my home to create a Map View is incredibly easy” on a 7-point scale. The scan had to reach 5.5, with the map still accurate.

### Worked ease and accuracy in the same cycles

Ease ratings and checks of the map against the real home changed the coaching, the flow and the editor in the same rounds, so one never improved at the other’s cost. The scan went one room at a time.

## How it worked

Before

### One list for every device

In September 2023, Amazon said customers had connected more than 400 million smart home devices to Alexa, and millions of them had more than 20. In the Alexa app, each device was a row in one list, found by its name.
Amazon’s devices event, 20 September 2023: the slide before Map View.
01 Scan

### Walk the room with the phone

A customer held up a Pro iPhone and walked one room at a time. White lines traced the walls and furniture as a small 3D model of the room grew on screen.
Map View’s scan, in Amazon’s 2023 film: white lines trace a kitchen.
02 Join

### Depth becomes a floor plan

The LiDAR scanner measured depth as the customer walked, and software on the phone found the walls, doors, windows and furniture. Camera images were processed on the phone and not stored. Each new room joined the last at the doorway the customer chose.
03 Place

### Drag each device onto its room

Lights, speakers, plugs and the thermostat became pins on the plan. Beta customers and research showed that seeing status at a glance mattered, so each pin showed its device’s live state from Alexa.
Map View in the Alexa app: each device on its room, with its state.
04 Control

### Tap the map to run the home

A tap on a pin sent the command through Alexa to the light, plug or thermostat. Every device on the map works: tap one to switch it.
A coffee maker’s plug switched from the map, in Amazon’s 2023 film.
Drawing of the flow, from Amazon’s published descriptions.

## Time to set up, as each source measured it

## Launch

Amazon’s press image for Map View’s launch, September 2023.
“Finally, no more scrolling through an endless list of devices.”
The Verge, on Map View’s launch
Announced on 20 September 2023 and launched in November 2023 for customers in the United States who had signed up. At CES in January 2024, Samsung, LG and TP-Link’s Tapo showed map-based controls of their own.

## What came next

On 28 October 2026, Amazon announced Alexa Home Map, a 3D successor that keeps Map View’s steps: scan each room, place each device, control it from the map. The Verge called it “a ground-up rebuild of the map view that launched in 2023.”
Alexa Home Map on an Echo Show 16, 2026.

Amazon Health AI

2021–2023 · Amazon Health AI

# Amazon Health AI

An organization that turned phone-camera images into health measures: body fat, waist‑to‑hip ratio, and mobility, stability and posture.
Halo Movement’s detailed results, 2021: mobility and stability by body region. · 1 / 2
Role
First product lead of Amazon’s Health Computer Vision and AI organization
Scale
100+ scientists and engineers; a $100M+ a year investment portfolio I directed
Validated
Three studies in npj Digital Medicine: [Body](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41746-022-00628-3) and [Movement](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41746-022-00684-9) in 2022, [waist-to-hip](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41746-023-00909-5) in 2023
I was the first product lead of Amazon’s Health Computer Vision and AI organization: 100+ scientists and engineers and a $100M+ a year portfolio. I tied further investment to two proofs: real customer value and a capability that worked. Three of its products were validated in npj Digital Medicine.

## What I decided

### Brought the leaders together on one direction

I brought the organization’s leaders together for three days to agree on one direction: using the camera in everyone’s phone to help people live healthier lives.

### Required two proofs before scaling investment

Each new capability needed both proofs: a customer problem stated without the technology, and experiments showing the capability worked. If either was missing, we paused further investment.

### Chose each measure’s clinical reference first

For each product, I chose the clinical reference by starting from the claim we needed to publish. All three studies appeared in npj Digital Medicine, a Nature Portfolio journal.

## How it worked

Before

### Every measure needed a clinic and an instrument

Body fat came from a clinical X-ray (DXA) scan, a movement assessment from a motion-capture suit and a physical therapist, and a waist-to-hip ratio from trained staff with a tape. Each needed a clinic and trained staff.
Each measure in a clinic, and with the phone.
01 Direction

### One organization, from research to products

In 2021 I became the first product lead of Amazon’s Health Computer Vision and AI organization, which ran from research and development to commercial products.
02 Measure

### What the camera asked, and what came back

Halo Body estimated body fat from phone photos, and from August 2021 its scan worked from the knees up, for members in smaller rooms. Halo Movement scored mobility, stability and posture from 0 to 100, from five exercises filmed by a phone on the floor. A third model estimated waist-to-hip ratio, a body-shape measure linked to disease risk, from three photos taken to voice prompts.
Halo Body’s result, in Amazon Science’s June 2021 article on how it worked: a 3D model and body fat.
03 Reference

### Each measure against its own reference

Body was tested against clinical DXA scans at two clinical sites, Movement against a motion-capture suit and clinical tests. The waist-to-hip model was tested against tape measurements by trained staff and laser body scans.

### Three products, three clinical references

Each product was checked against its own clinical reference.
The data as a table
Product · The phone saw · Checked against · The result · Published
Body · Front and back photos · DXA, a clinical X-ray scan · About half the error of the best smart scale · npj Digital Medicine, June 2022
Movement · Video of five exercises · A motion-capture suit and 13 clinical tests · Told apart athletes, healthy adults and adults with impaired movement · npj Digital Medicine, September 2022
Waist-to-hip · Front, side and back photos · Tape measures by trained staff · About half the error of people measuring themselves · npj Digital Medicine, September 2023
04 Gate

### Friday builds with a 1% chance of working

Some ideas started as Friday builds: each Friday a product manager, a designer and a group of engineers took on one charter, “build something that won’t work.” We chose builds with about a 1% chance of working and a tenfold gain on a business metric if they did.

## Launch

On 28 September 2022, at Amazon’s devices event, I introduced Halo Rise, a bedside sleep tracker built by Amazon’s Halo Rise team.

## What came next

The waist-to-hip study was published in September 2023. In June 2024 I published the method we ran, in an essay for product managers building consumer AI products.
From the 2023 paper: the app’s waist-to-hip ratio against tape measurements by trained staff.

Halo Movement
2019–2021

---

Page: Halo Movement | Njenga Kariuki
Address: https://njenga.ai/halo-movement/

2019–2021 · Amazon Halo

# Halo Movement

An assessment of mobility, stability and posture from phone video, with a personal exercise program to improve them.
Amazon’s results screen, June 2021: an overall score of 71, “Good.”
Role
Product lead for Movement, end to end
Validated
[npj Digital Medicine, 2022](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-022-00684-9)
Result
More than 80% of members who exercised for two weeks improved
I led Halo Movement end to end: a movement score and program from phone video. I set the score to match a movement expert’s judgment, and cut 10 to 15 exercises to five. Of members who exercised for two weeks, more than 80% improved.

## What I decided

### Set the score to match an expert’s judgment

I set the target as the score a movement expert would give. Experts annotated example videos with each error and its severity. A published study then checked the score against motion capture and clinical tests.

### Cut 10 to 15 exercises to five

Our fitness experts first proposed 10 to 15 exercises, and many were hard for ordinary people. With the computer vision team, I cut the set to five and kept the score aligned with an expert’s.

### Built real-time feedback into the workouts

We built real-time feedback into the workouts to make them dynamic, accurate and rich, which motivated people once they had a score. When members asked for more variety in that feedback, we made variety a measured dimension.

## How it worked

Before

### A movement screen needed a professional

Everyone wants to improve their mobility. A full clinical screen needed a physical therapist and equipment: a goniometer to measure joint angles, foam pads, a hurdle and a plumb line. My goal was a professional-grade mobility assessment and personal exercises, at home, with only a phone.
01 Film

### Five movements, filmed on the phone

A member stood the phone on the floor, leveled it with an on-screen guide, and stepped back into a square framing the body. Five movements followed, including a single-leg balance and an overhead squat, in under 10 minutes. The video was encrypted, analyzed in Amazon’s cloud within seconds and deleted, and no person saw it.
The app’s setup screen in the 2022 study, redrawn: the phone ready to record.
02 Score

### A score out of 100, from the errors an expert would see

Weighted errors became scores for mobility, stability and posture, by body area. The scale ran up to Olympic athletes, so even the most athletic people using Halo would rarely score above 90.

### What a score of 81 meant

A score made sense beside the 2022 study’s three groups: athletes, healthy adults and adults with impaired movement.
The data as a table
Average score by group in the 2022 study
Group · Average score
Athletes · About 87
Healthy adults · About 81
Adults with impaired movement · About 68
03 Program

### A program aimed at the errors found

The same errors chose the corrective exercises in the member’s program: five to seven routines from a library of 35 corrective exercises by the physical therapist Kelly Starrett, each 5 to 10 minutes, at least three times a week.
04 Reassess

### A new assessment after two weeks

The app recommended two weeks of exercises before a new assessment. Of members who did the recommended exercises for two weeks and reassessed, more than 80% improved.
Amazon’s Movement Health explainer, 2021.
A drawing of the idea.

## Launch

Amazon’s graphic announcing Movement, June 2021: “Tools to improve the way you move.”
“Like having a personal trainer and physical therapist in your pocket”
TODAY (NBC News), the day after Movement went live
Amazon announced Movement Health on 3 June 2021. It went live on 30 June 2021, included in the $3.99-a-month Halo membership.

## What came next

On 6 September 2022, npj Digital Medicine, a Nature Portfolio journal, published the validation study. The score separated athletes, healthy adults and adults with impaired movement.

Halo Tone
2018–2021

---

Page: Halo Tone | Njenga Kariuki
Address: https://njenga.ai/halo-tone/

2018–2021 · Amazon Halo

# Halo Tone

The Halo Band sampled the wearer’s voice; the phone showed how it sounded to others, in words such as “Hopeful.”
Launch illustration of Tone, 2020: the day’s tones and two notable moments. · 1 / 2
Role
Led Tone end to end, from the listener panels to launch
Patents
Six US patents, granted 2022 to 2026
Launched
August 2020, in the United States
I led Halo Tone end to end: how your voice sounds to others, analyzed on the phone. I defined what that meant, built the listener panels that taught the model, and set the audio sampling the band’s battery was designed around. Six US patents came from it.

## What I decided

### Took the training labels from listener panels

How a voice sounds to others is a judgment people make, so the model’s labels came from listener panels. I defined what the panels rated and how they were built.

### Sampled the least audio a result needed

I worked back from the least audio a meaningful result needed. That became the hardware team’s requirement for the band’s battery and size. Three of the six patents describe this sampling.

### Replaced four labels with two scores and words

The first model aimed at accuracy on four labels: happy, sad, low energy and high energy. Playing results back to customers did not work: people wanted to know what a result meant. So we moved to two continuous scores and plain words.

## How it worked

Before

### No measure for how you come across

Social well-being affects long-term health, and there was no good measure of it. Tone began with a demo that placed the voices of two US presidents on two axes, energy and positivity. The two voices fell far apart.
01 Rate

### Listeners rated the clips the model learned from

Panels of listeners rated short clips from happy to sad and from low to high energy. Their ratings became the labels the model learned from. Amazon said its employees rated tens of thousands of voices across US regions and demographic groups.
Each listener rates the same clip; together their ratings set its label.
02 Score

### Two scores for every stretch of speech

The model gave each stretch of speech two scores: positivity, how happy or sad it sounded, and energy, how excited or tired. In live mode, the voice moved around a positivity and energy graph with each word.

### Two scores, one word

Tone placed each voice reading on two scales, energy and positivity, and named its region with a word, such as content or irritated.
Illustration
The data as a table
The word for each region of energy and positivity
Word · Energy · Positivity · Other words
Excited · Higher · Higher · amused, delighted
Content · Lower · Higher · appreciative, caring
Worried · Lower · Lower · reserved, discouraged
Irritated · Higher · Lower · displeased, enraged
03 Describe

### Plain words for the day, such as “Hopeful”

Tone showed the day’s moments as plain words with times, such as “Hopeful” at 10:30 AM. Customers wanted to see how their voice varied, so we made that variation a measured dimension.
Amazon’s Halo launch film, 2020: the day’s notable moments, each a word and a time.
04 Sample

### Sample just enough voice to save the battery

The band sampled speech at intervals through the day, which saved its battery. In the patents’ example, a wearable that listens nonstop lasts under 10 hours on a charge. One that sleeps between checks lasts 2 days or more.
Battery life on one charge, in the patents’ example.
05 Protect

### Only the wearer’s voice, and no audio kept

I defined the path from band to phone and balanced its privacy and legal requirements so Tone could launch. The band sent short, encrypted segments to the phone, which kept only the wearer’s speech, analyzed it and deleted the audio. Only positivity and energy summaries reached Amazon’s cloud, and no one heard a recording.
The audio’s path: what leaves each step gets smaller.

## Six US patents, by grant date

Drawn from each patent

## Launch

“I found the Tone feature to be eerily accurate”
Android Central’s review of Amazon Halo, September 2020
Tone launched with Amazon Halo on 27 August 2020, in early access in the United States.

## What came next

Amazon’s next band, Halo View, announced in September 2021, had no microphone; its owners ran Tone live on the phone.

Halo Body
2018–2021

---

Page: Halo Body | Njenga Kariuki
Address: https://njenga.ai/halo-body/

2018–2021 · Amazon Halo

# Halo Body

A phone scan that returned a member’s body fat percentage and a 3D model of their body.
Halo Body at launch, 2020: a member’s 3D model, body fat and weight.
Role
Product lead for Body, end to end
Validated
[npj Digital Medicine, 2022](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-022-00628-3)
Accuracy
About half the error of the best smart scale, against a clinical scan
I led Halo Body end to end: body fat and a 3D model from a phone scan. Amazon’s CEO set the challenge, a scan close to the best body fat scanners. I moved its training labels to clinical instruments; in the published study its error was about half the best smart scale’s.

## What I decided

### Started from the claim we could publish

I started from what the customer would read: an accuracy claim we could publish. A claim measured against the most accurate scanners needed their readings to learn from.

### Moved the training labels to clinical instruments

Our first models learned from fitness experts who judged body fat by eye. We changed the labels to readings from reference instruments: the model we validated learned from the body fat values of clinical X-ray (DXA) scans and never saw the images.

### Made the scan itself part of quality

Feedback showed the scan itself was part of the quality members perceived, so we measured and improved it. From August 2021, members could stand about 1 to 2 feet (30 to 60 centimeters) closer, so Body worked in smaller rooms.

## How it worked

Before

### An accurate body fat number needed a clinic

In 2020, measuring body fat accurately meant a DXA scan in a clinic, with a doctor’s prescription. An accurate scan cost people $75 to $150, a price we judged too high for customers.
01 Capture

### Four coached photos, in any room

The aim was a fully automatic phone scan that worked at home, in any room and any light. A member stood 4 to 6 feet (1.2 to 1.8 meters) from the phone, in tight, minimal clothing, for four coached photos: front, back and each side.

### The capture coach, step by step

The app coached four photos, checking the phone’s level, the distance and the pose, so any room could produce a usable scan.
Illustration
The data as a table
The four steps of a scan
Step · What the app coached
Level · The phone stands upright on a surface, about knee to waist high.
Distance · The member steps back, about 4 to 6 feet (1.2 to 1.8 m).
Pose · Arms and legs move into the outline on the screen.
Photos · Four photos: front, back, left and right.
02 Analyze

### Three neural networks, results in seconds

In Amazon’s cloud, one neural network separated the person from the room. A second read body fat from the front and back photos only, and a third built a 3D model from the silhouettes. Results came back in seconds.
03 Show

### A 3D model, a number and a slider

Each member saw a 3D model of their own body beside their body fat percentage. A slider showed the same body at more or less body fat. The Verge, a technology news site, wrote that the slider “could also be literally dangerous for people with body dysmorphic disorder.” From launch day it stopped at the bottom of a healthy range for the member’s sex and age, and Body was for adults only.
The same body at less body fat, down to the slider’s floor: a drawing of the idea.
04 Test

### Tested at two clinics against DXA

Massachusetts General Hospital and Pennington Biomedical Research Center tested Body in a blinded study. Its average error against DXA was the lowest of seven methods, and stayed the lowest in every group by sex, body mass index and race. Amazon saw no DXA result until Body’s estimates were with the investigators, and the model had never trained on clinic data.
Amazon’s Halo launch film, 2020.
A drawing of the idea.

## Average error against a clinical X-ray scan (DXA), in points

2022 study

## Launch

Amazon’s launch illustration, 2020: a scan at home, and the 3D model it returns.
“Amazon’s Halo passes Pennington’s test for accurately measuring percentage of body fat”
The Advocate, on the study’s results, June 2021
Body launched with Halo on 27 August 2020. The study’s results came out on 16 June 2021, and npj Digital Medicine, a Nature Portfolio journal, published the paper on 29 June 2022.

## What came next

In September 2022, an independent study tested Body against a reference more thorough than DXA, and only Body’s estimate passed. In 2025, four obesity and nutrition societies cited the 2022 study in an advisory on nutrition during GLP-1 obesity treatment.

Amazon Halo
2018–2021

---

Page: Amazon Halo | Njenga Kariuki
Address: https://njenga.ai/halo/

2018–2021 · Amazon Health AI

# Amazon Halo

Amazon’s first health wearable: a band with no screen, paired with an app and a membership.
The Halo Band in its three launch colors, 2020. · 1 / 3
Role
Product lead for Body, Tone and Movement, on Halo’s founding team
Patents
6 US patents, 2022 to 2026
Launched
August 2020
I joined Amazon Halo’s founding team in 2018 as the one product owner for Body, Tone and Movement: three health measures from a band and a phone. I set what each model was trained and checked against, and launched them in 2020 and 2021.

## What I decided

### Set what each model was checked against

For Body, Tone and Movement, I set what each model was trained and checked against: clinical X-ray scans of body fat, listener panels’ ratings of recorded voices, and the score a fitness expert would give.

### Measured value at first use and weeks later

Novelty lifts a first rating, so we measured the value members saw in a result at first use, and again at about 2 and 4 weeks. Groups of people new to the product gave fast feedback on each change.

### Judged the models on real-world data

What people perceived in the lab and at home differed sharply, so we judged the models on real-world data.

## How it worked

Before

### Health measures that needed a clinic

An accurate body fat reading needed a clinical X-ray scan and a doctor’s prescription. A full movement screen needed a physical therapist and equipment.
01 Wear

### A band with no screen, and one app

The band had no display, notifications or clock: everything a member saw appeared in the app. Its home screen held four tiles: Activity, Sleep, Tone and Body.
The band and the Halo app, December 2020.
02 Measure

### Three AI measures from a band and a phone

Body estimated body fat and built a 3D model of the member’s body from phone photos. Tone used words such as “hopeful” to describe how the wearer’s voice sounded to others. From June 2021, Movement scored mobility, stability and posture out of 100 from five movements filmed on the phone.
Body, Tone and Movement as members saw them in the app, 2020 and 2021.
03 Split

### Analyzed on the phone or in the cloud, then deleted

Tone’s audio went from the band’s microphones to the phone, which analyzed and deleted it; only a summary reached the cloud. Body’s photos and Movement’s videos were processed in Amazon’s cloud, then deleted.
Where each measure was analyzed, and where its data was deleted.
04 Repeat

### A new result every few weeks

Amazon recommended a Body scan every 2 weeks and a new Movement assessment every 2 to 4 weeks. In December 2020, Amazon added Insights from early-access feedback: trends such as a member’s peak periods of positivity.
Body screen, 2021: the 3D model and a trend chart of body fat.

## Launch

Amazon’s illustration introducing Halo, August 2020: the app’s Activity, Sleep, Tone and Body tiles.
“Amazon’s first health wearable is no Fitbit or Apple Watch clone”
Fast Company, on Halo’s launch day
Amazon announced Halo on 27 August 2020, with invitation-only early access, and opened it to all US customers on 14 December 2020. The band cost $99.99 with 6 months of membership; after that, membership cost $3.99 a month.

## What came next

Amazon ended Halo in 2023. The app was rated close to 4.5 stars, and its AI features set it apart, but it worked only with a Halo band. In a crowded wearables market, a place on the customer’s wrist was hard to earn. What I took from it: distribution sets a product’s ceiling as much as its quality does. An app that also worked with the Apple Watch or Fitbit a customer already wore could have earned a subscription of its own. Hearing how you sound to others, or measuring body fat close to a clinical scan from a phone, would still stand out today.

Alexa Shopping
2017–2018

---

Page: Alexa Shopping | Njenga Kariuki
Address: https://njenga.ai/alexa-shopping/

2017–2018 · Alexa, Amazon

# Alexa Shopping

Ordering by voice on an Echo speaker: one spoken request, one offer read back, then a “yes.”
A voice order, drawn from Amazon’s 2017 examples.
Role
First product lead for how Alexa understood shopping requests
Team
Built and led a 10-person evaluation team
Result
Shopping success from about 50% to 85%
I was the first product lead for how Alexa understood shopping requests. Alexa’s overall measures said shopping worked; I set out to test that. I listened to 1,000 requests a week and wrote how each would be judged. Success rose from about 50% to 85%.

## What I decided

### Judged each request by its one offer

A request counted as a success only when Alexa’s one offer was the product the customer asked for. Shopping success was the share of sampled requests that met that bar.

### Held a 10-person team to one written standard

Each type of error had a written definition and a set of examples, so 10 people would judge the same request the same way. When the team found a case the rubric did not cover, we added it. The models learned from the team’s judgments.

### Ranked one customer measure above model measures

Three steps that are each 90% accurate leave about one customer in four with an error. So shopping success ranked above model measures such as speech recognition accuracy.

## How it worked

Before

### One request, one offer, no screen

A customer could say “Alexa, order,” name a product, hear one offer with Prime delivery, and say “yes.” An Echo speaker had no screen and no list of results, so only that offer counted. A request could break at any step: a misheard brand, the wrong task or the wrong offer.
Echo Plus, drawn: the light ring glows when Alexa hears its wake word.
01 Hear

### Brand names were easy to mishear

Speech recognition in Amazon’s cloud turned the sound into words. Brand names were easy to mishear, and a speaker could not suggest completions the way a search box does. In one published case, background noise turned “epilepsy bracelets” into “apple upci uhhh bracelets.”
02 Understand

### The same words could mean another task

Language understanding models then decided what the customer wanted done, and which words named the product. The same verb could mean different tasks; Amazon’s own 2018 example was “order me a cab” and “order me an Echo Dot.” Fixing one could weaken the other.
Labels on each word let Alexa split one spoken request into separate list items. Drawn from an Amazon Science example, 2018.
03 Offer

### Only the one offer counted

Alexa offered an item from the customer’s order history first, then an Amazon’s Choice product, popular and well priced, then the top search result. In one of Amazon’s 2017 examples, “Alexa, order Bose Soundlink three,” an offer of any other model was a wrong order.
04 Judge

### Judge every request, then fix what failed

Each week I listened to 1,000 sampled interactions and marked every turn, one request and Alexa’s reply, a success or a failure. From that listening I wrote the rubric, the written guide to what counted as success, with examples. Each failure went to the scientists and engineers who could fix it, in quick rounds. I led the fine-tuning of Alexa’s base language model for shopping requests.

### One request, judged by its offer

Under my rubric, a spoken shopping request succeeded only if Alexa offered the product the customer asked for.
Example
The data as a table
“Alexa, order Bose Soundlink three.” Three example replies, judged
Alexa’s reply · Where it broke · Words the offer kept · Judged
The requested Bose SoundLink model, with price, then a request to confirm · Nowhere · Bose, Soundlink, three · Success. The customer gets the speaker they asked for.
A different Bose SoundLink model · Understand · Bose, Soundlink · Failure. The customer would get the wrong speaker.
A reply that no matching product was found · Offer · None · Failure. The customer gets no product.

## Sampled shopping requests that ended in the right offer

## What came next

In December 2018, Amazon said customers’ use of Alexa for shopping had more than tripled from 2017. In May 2026, Amazon combined its Rufus and Alexa+ assistants into Alexa for Shopping, which works by voice, touch or both.
Sources

Prime Now
2015–2017

---

Page: Prime Now | Njenga Kariuki
Address: https://njenga.ai/prime-now/

2015–2017 · Prime Now, Amazon

# Prime Now

How local stores with no online business sold through Prime Now, which delivered within one or two hours.
Choosing a delivery window at launch, December 2014, redrawn. · 1 / 3
Role
Founding product manager of the local-store and seller platform
Reach
Partner stores in 7 countries by 2017
Result
Out of stock from 25% to 5%; 40 hours a week of manual work automated
I was the founding product manager of Prime Now’s platform for local stores and sellers. I sat in the first stores, took the spreadsheets they had, then learned to code and automated the rest. Out of stock at partner stores fell from 25% to 5%.

## What I decided

### Took whatever data each store had

The stores had never sold online, so I asked for what they had: “Send me spreadsheets, whatever you have.” For six months I uploaded their files by hand, starting at 4 AM, and updated them four times a day.

### Synced every store’s stock to the app daily

I built a system that matched each store’s items to Amazon’s catalog, produced forecasts and uploaded its stock every day. Out of stock at partner stores fell from 25% to 5%.

### Measured each new country on its growth

As Prime Now opened in new countries, each was measured on revenue, a goal that did not reward growing two-hour delivery. I proposed measuring each country on its percentage growth, and leadership adopted it.

## How it worked

Before

### Delivery within the hour needed the item on the shelf

Prime Now began selling goods from local stores on 21 May 2015, starting in Manhattan. Until then it had sold only Amazon’s own stock. The stores had never sold online: no online catalog, no product feed and no way to send their stock to an app. Delivery within the hour worked only if the item the app showed was on the shelf when the order came in.
01 Collect

### Take each store’s spreadsheet as it came

Each store sent its items in whatever file it kept. Packaged goods carried barcodes, loose produce carried four- or five-digit codes for its kind, and everything else carried the store’s own item codes. PCC, a Seattle grocer, put 10,000 or more items into the app.
02 Match

### Match each item to Amazon’s catalog

The system built each store’s catalog by matching its items to Amazon’s products by algorithm. Loose produce and a store’s own brands had no record to find, so they needed new ones. In Madrid in September 2016, partner stores brought 7,000 products, 5,000 of them new to Prime Now.
03 Forecast

### A forecast for every store

The system produced forecasts for each store. Lavinia, a Paris wine merchant, said Amazon supplied it with forecasts based on Amazon’s experience in other European countries.
04 Upload

### Upload every store’s stock every day

Each day the system uploaded every store’s stock to the app automatically. Each daily upload closed the gap that had opened between the app and the shelf. The system automated 40 hours of manual work a week.
I also designed the payment and fulfillment APIs that independent sellers used, carrying millions of transactions.
A drawing of the system.

## Out of stock at partner stores

## What came next

In 2021 Amazon retired the Prime Now app and moved fast delivery into its main app. Partner stores such as Bartell’s, Morrisons and Monoprix moved with it. In December 2025 Amazon began testing a successor, Amazon Now, with delivery in about 30 minutes.
Amazon Now, Prime Now’s 30-minute successor, 2026.
Sources

Amazon Bedding & Bath
2014–2015

---

Page: Amazon Bedding & Bath | Njenga Kariuki
Address: https://njenga.ai/bedding-and-bath/

2014–2015 · Amazon Retail

# Amazon Bedding & Bath

Amazon’s own business in sheets, towels and pillows: goods bought wholesale from brands and sold beside independent sellers.
A sale’s price, from the cost of goods to the margin, with the margin’s edge under a loupe: a drawing of the idea.
Role
Vendor manager, owner of the business’s profit and loss
P&L
$100M+ a year
Review
Every weekly margin change, explained to a hundredth of a percentage point
I owned the profit and loss of Amazon’s Bedding & Bath business, more than $100 million a year. I led the negotiations with its brands, set the supply-chain terms, and explained every weekly margin change to a hundredth of a percentage point.

## What I decided

### Negotiated cost and funding with the brands

I led the negotiations with the category’s brands, over the cost of each item and the funding each brand gave Amazon. Both moved the margin I explained every week.

### Set the terms for stock and shipping

I set the supply-chain terms: how much stock to hold, and how each item shipped. When FedEx and UPS began pricing every ground parcel by its size, a comforter’s box became a cost to negotiate.

### Explained every margin change, every week

Every week, in the business review, I explained each change in the category’s margin, down to one basis point: a hundredth of a percentage point.

## How it worked

Before

### A $100M+ P&L, explained weekly to a hundredth of a point

Amazon bought sheets, towels and pillows wholesale from brands, owned the stock, set the price and shipped each order. On each product page, Amazon’s own offer sat beside offers from independent sellers. In 2014 those sellers sold more than 40% of Amazon’s units.
01 Funding

### Brand funding counted as a lower cost of goods

Brands funded marketing, promotions and volume rebates, and Amazon booked that money as a lower cost of goods. A rebate usually depended on buying a minimum volume. Vendor managers also negotiated deals with their brands, such as holiday discounts.
Brand funding, booked as a lower cost of goods.
02 Ship

### Carriers began pricing every parcel by its size

From the turn of 2015, FedEx and UPS priced every ground parcel by its size as well as its weight. Light, bulky goods such as comforters cost more to ship.
Shipping, priced by parcel size as well as weight from January 2015.
03 Forecast

### Machine-learning forecasts, which managers could override

A vendor manager decided how much of each item to place in each Amazon warehouse, and when. Machine-learning forecasts sat in the vendor manager’s tools. A vendor manager could override them. For example, a manager could raise an order before a brand’s marketing push the forecast did not expect.
A manager’s order, raised ahead of a marketing push.

## What came next

In 2015 I moved from Bedding & Bath to Prime Now, which delivered within one or two hours.
Sources

Target

Page: Target | Njenga Kariuki
Address: https://njenga.ai/target-apple/

2012–2014 · Target, Apple category

# Target

The supply chain for Apple products at Target: iPads, iPods and accessories, stocked store by store.
iPad mini, launched November 2012, and iPad Air, launched November 2013.
Role
Senior supply chain analyst, owner of supply-chain strategy for the Apple category
Scale
A $700M+ a year category across about 1,800 stores
Result
In-stock rate up 24%; market share up 3%
I owned supply-chain strategy for Target’s $700M+ Apple category across about 1,800 stores. I changed how systems built for everyday goods stocked Apple products, store by store, and allocated the iPad mini launch to each store. The in-stock rate rose 24% and market share 3%.

## What I decided

### Changed how systems stocked Apple, store by store

I changed how Target’s systems stocked Apple products, store by store, for one of the company’s largest businesses.

### Launched the 2012 Apple shop-in-shop rollout

I launched the rollout of the Apple shop-in-shop in 2012. One of the first shops carried most of Apple’s line, with a Target employee trained on Apple products.

### Allocated the iPad mini launch to each store

I managed the most important allocation of Apple products at Target, for the iPad mini’s launch on 2 November 2012. Online ship times were about two weeks, Target’s included, so the units on each shelf were the units most shoppers could buy.

## How it worked

Before

### Apple products on systems built for shampoo

The category held the iPads, iPods and accessories on Target’s shelves. Its retail systems were set up for everyday goods such as shampoo and toothpaste. Most of its goods moved through its distribution centers.
01 Shops

### From two Apple shops to about two dozen

In January 2012 Target confirmed a test of Apple shops inside 25 of its stores. Two were open by early May, and about two dozen by August.
02 Allocate

### Each store’s share, with no sales history

Allocation decided how many units each store received. Apple launch units went direct to each store, outside the distribution centers. A new product such as the iPad mini had no sales history, and once a store sold out, its sales stopped measuring demand.
Each store’s share of the launch units, sent direct from Apple: one dot per store, the shares a drawing of the idea.
03 Launch

### Too few iPad minis, 21 days before Black Friday

The iPad mini went on sale on 2 November 2012, 21 days before Black Friday, which opens the US holiday shopping season. Fortune reported that white iPad mini pre-orders sold out in about 20 minutes. Apple later said it could not make enough of them in any week of the holiday quarter. The fight to allocate was intense.
The 21 days from the iPad mini’s launch to Black Friday, 2012.
04 Peak

### iPads were Target’s top three Black Friday items

On Black Friday 2013, a shopper panel put Apple products at about 22% of Target’s early sales. Target’s three best-selling single items were all iPads, led by the iPad Air.
Black Friday 2013, in a shopper panel’s receipts.

## Change while I ran the category

In-stock rate · Up 24%
Market share · Up 3%

## What came next

In February 2021 Target introduced Apple at Target shops in 17 stores. It told CNBC that it had tested more prominent Apple displays nearly a decade earlier, and that the new shops went much further. By October 2022 they were in more than 150 stores.
Sources
